questions.q: What is a "data set" within a BI Publisher data model?
options: A visual layout template
A query against a data source that returns the rows and columns needed for the report
A dashboard page
A duty role controlling catalog access
questions.explain: A data set is essentially a query (often against predefined view objects or a subject area) that returns the data a report needs.

questions.q: What role do parameters play in a BI Publisher data model?
options: They define the report's visual font and layout
They let a user supply values, such as a date range or business unit, that flow into the query as filter conditions before the report runs
They are only used in OTBI, never in BI Publisher
They permanently alter the data model's structure
questions.explain: Parameters let the same report definition run against different slices of data without editing the underlying query each time.

questions.q: Why would a data model use a header data set and a separate, linked detail data set (such as for company info plus invoice line items)?
options: To intentionally produce unrelated, duplicate data
So the combined XML nests detail rows correctly beneath their corresponding header for the template to lay out properly
Because BI Publisher does not support more than one data set
To avoid ever needing an XML structure
questions.explain: Linking data sets (e.g., by invoice ID) produces a properly nested XML structure that a template can lay out as a header followed by repeating detail rows.

questions.q: What format is the final output of a data model, regardless of its underlying sources?
options: A PDF file
An RTF template
XML
A Financial Reporting Studio grid
questions.explain: Whatever the data model's sources and structure, it ultimately produces XML, which is what a template consumes to produce the final laid-out output.

questions.q: Why does getting the data set structure right matter for the template that will be built later?
options: It doesn't matter; templates can reshape any XML automatically
A template can only lay out the XML shape it's actually given, so a poorly structured data model forces awkward workarounds in the template
Templates are built before data models, so structure is irrelevant
XML structure only affects OTBI, not BI Publisher
questions.explain: Because templates lay out the specific shape of the XML they receive, a well-structured data model avoids unnecessary complexity at the template-building stage.
